content: Your doctor has prescribed fat emulsions to serve as a source of calories and essential fatty acids to help maintain or increase your body weight. This medication will be diluted in a total parenteral nutrition (TPN) solution or placed in a separate container and administered through a needle or catheter inserted into your vein. The infusion will typically last for at least 4 to 6 hours daily or may be delivered continuously over a 24-hour period. Your healthcare provider, which may include your doctor, nurse, or pharmacist, will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and check for side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your body responds to the medication. Before starting fat emulsion therapy, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to fat emulsions, eggs (as one of the ingredients in fat emulsions is derived from eggs), soybean oil, safflower oil, or any other medications. Additionally, let them know about all prescription and nonprescription medications you are currently taking, including vitamins. Inform your doctor if you have a history of kidney disease or diabetes. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. Should you become pregnant while receiving fat emulsion therapy, contact your doctor immediately. Before administering the fat emulsion, carefully inspect the solution. It should not contain any floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or examine the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it appears discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your provider. If you experience a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. If this occurs, contact your provider immediately to ensure your therapy can continue without interruption. Fat emulsions may cause side effects. If you experience symptoms such as vomiting, shivering, fever, or chills, contact your healthcare provider immediately. In the event of a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days’ worth of fat emulsion at a time. You may be instructed to store the medication in the refrigerator or at room temperature. Before using your next dose, remove it from the refrigerator one hour in advance and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to warm to room temperature. Store the medication only as directed and ensure you understand the proper storage requirements. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and ensure all medications and supplies are out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will provide instructions on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving fat emulsions through a vein or under your skin, it is important to recognize the signs of a catheter-related infection. This type of infection occurs at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin.
